blocks.eyebrow: HUGHES ROOM VIEWS · THE LIVING WORLD
blocks.title:
The hidden
world of fungi.
blocks.intro: A mushroom is only part of the story. Step into a world of tiny spores, secret threads, and surprising science.

blocks.title: Small. Strange. Extraordinary.
blocks.intro: Fungi aren’t plants or animals. They belong to a kingdom of their own. Meet three very different examples. These pictures show different zoom levels.

cards.title: Mushroom makers
cards.body: Some fungi grow mushrooms: the parts that make and release spores.

media.alt: A group of small blue Mycena interrupta mushrooms growing among moss and wood.
media.caption: Real blue mushrooms! These are Mycena interrupta, photographed in Tasmania.

cards.title: Fuzzy moulds
cards.body: Many moulds grow as tiny branching threads. That fuzz is a fungus growing!

media.alt: Fine pale Rhizopus mould threads on a strawberry, topped by tiny dark round spore cases.
media.caption: Look for the tiny dark dots. They are spore cases on Rhizopus mould.

cards.title: Tiny yeasts
cards.body: Yeasts are fungi too. They usually live as single cells, too small to see on their own.

media.alt: Oval Saccharomyces cerevisiae yeast cells seen with a microscope; several have small buds.
media.caption: A microscope brings these yeast cells into view. Some have a tiny bud growing from them.

blocks.title: There’s more under that cap.
blocks.intro: Tap a numbered point to investigate this gilled mushroom. Other mushrooms can have different shapes and parts.

hotspots.label: Cap
hotspots.body: The cap holds the spore-making surface underneath it. Look below the umbrella!

hotspots.label: Gills
hotspots.body: These thin plates under the cap make spores. Not all mushrooms have gills.

hotspots.label: Stem
hotspots.body: The stem lifts the cap. This helps spores reach moving air.

hotspots.label: Mycelium
hotspots.body: These branching threads are part of the fungus. A single thread is called a hypha. A network of threads is mycelium.

hotspots.label: Spores
hotspots.body: Spores can start new fungal growth when conditions are right. They are enlarged here so we can see them.

detailMedia.alt: A real close-up of the thin ridges under a mushroom cap, radiating out from its stem.
detailMedia.caption: Follow the ridges under a real mushroom cap. These are its gills.

blocks.title: The mushroom is just the beginning.
blocks.intro: What could be growing where we can’t see? Switch views, then grow the branching threads.

media.alt: White cottony mycelium spreading in a branching patch over a piece of wood.
media.caption: Real mycelium on wood. Can you find where the fine threads spread out?

views.label: Above the surface
views.body: We notice the mushroom. It is a fruiting body: the spore-making part of this fungus.

views.label: Below the surface
views.body: Mycelium can grow through soil or inside wood. Its threads branch as they grow and absorb food from their surroundings.

blocks.title: Tiny travellers. A huge adventure.
blocks.intro: How do spores get away from a mushroom? Try the wind tunnel, then follow a simplified mushroom life cycle.

steps.title: A spore lands
steps.body: In a suitable place, a spore can start growing a tiny thread.

steps.title: Threads spread
steps.body: Threads grow and branch into mycelium. For many mushroom makers, compatible threads must join before fruiting is possible.

steps.title: A mushroom grows
steps.body: With suitable conditions, the fungus may grow a mushroom. Not every spore gets this far!

steps.title: Spores set off
steps.body: A gilled mushroom releases spores from its gills. Once clear of the cap, they can drift on air currents.

blocks.title: The forest has a behind-the-scenes crew.
blocks.intro: Different fungi do different jobs. Some recycle, some team up with plants, and some help make our food.

cards.title: The recyclers
cards.body: Some fungi break down dead wood and leaves. Nutrients return to the environment and can be used again.

cards.title: The plant partners
cards.body: Some fungi exchange with plant roots: the fungus helps gather nutrients, and the plant supplies sugars.

cards.title: The tiny bakers
cards.body: Baker’s yeast makes carbon dioxide gas. Those little gas bubbles help bread dough rise.

blocks.title: Light. Electricity. A little mystery.
blocks.intro: Real discoveries can be stranger than stories. Explore what we know—and a question scientists are still investigating.

experiments.title: A living night-light
experiments.body: Some fungi make light through a chemical reaction. This is called bioluminescence. Most fungi do not glow.

media.alt: Panellus stipticus mushrooms emitting a green glow in the dark in a long-exposure photograph.
media.caption: Real glowing fungi: Panellus stipticus. The camera collected light for over eight minutes to make the glow easier to see.

experiments.title: Can we hear a pattern?
experiments.body: Scientists have measured electrical changes in fungi. What those changes do is still being studied. A change on a graph is not proof of a message.

blocks.title: Take a little wonder with you.
blocks.intro: Try a few discoveries, then test your explorer thinking.

cards.title: A ring with a reason
cards.body: Some mycelium grows outward in a circle. Mushrooms appearing around its edge can make a “fairy ring”.

cards.title: A tiny launch
cards.body: Many gilled mushrooms use a tiny drop of liquid to help launch each spore away from a gill.

cards.title: An unexpected relative
cards.body: Fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. They still have their very own kingdom!

choices.label: The plant kingdom
choices.feedback: A good question to investigate! Fungi have their own kingdom.

choices.label: A kingdom of their own
choices.feedback: You found it! Fungi belong to their own kingdom.

choices.label: A plant’s roots
choices.feedback: It can look root-like, but mycelium is part of a fungus.

choices.label: A network of fungal threads
choices.feedback: Exactly! One thread is a hypha. A network of them is mycelium.

questions.prompt: Can a mushroom’s colour tell us it is safe to eat?

choices.label: Yes, bright ones are the dangerous ones
choices.feedback: Colour cannot tell us. Safe and poisonous mushrooms can look very similar. Never taste a wild mushroom.

choices.label: No. Colour is not a safety test.
choices.feedback: That’s careful explorer thinking. Never taste a wild mushroom. Ask a trusted adult.

blocks.title: Now it’s our turn to wonder.
blocks.intro: Our growing story will live here: photographs, observations, and discoveries from the classroom.
